nameStory: Kamchatka Stonecrop gets its name from the Kamchatka Peninsula in far eastern Russia, one of its native homes. The 'stonecrop' part comes from these plants' amazing ability to grow in rocky crevices and stone walls where almost nothing else can survive. It's also called orange stonecrop for its bright golden-orange flowers that really pop against gray stone.
description: Kamchatka Stonecrop is a low-growing, carpet-forming succulent that spreads across the ground like a living mat. This hardy perennial typically stays under 6 inches tall but can spread several feet wide, creating dense patches of thick, fleshy leaves. In late summer, it bursts into bloom with clusters of bright orange-yellow star-shaped flowers that seem to glow against the green foliage. Originally from Asia, this tough little plant has escaped from rock gardens and now grows wild in some New England locations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright orange-yellow star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals appear in dense, flat-topped clusters in late summer. Each flower is small but they group together to create showy displays that feel almost electric in their intensity.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves that feel like tiny water balloons when squeezed gently. They're arranged in opposite pairs along the stems and have scalloped or toothed edges that give them a decorative appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height but spreading outward like a living carpet. Stems root where they touch the ground, helping the plant colonize new areas.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: All parts of the plant feel succulent and slightly rubbery, storing water in their tissues. The leaves have a waxy coating that makes them feel smooth and slightly slippery when wet.

habitat: In New England, Kamchatka Stonecrop is most often found as an escape from cultivation around old homesites, rock gardens, and stone walls. It thrives in well-drained, rocky soils and can tolerate poor, thin soils where other plants struggle. Look for it in sunny to partially shaded spots, especially on slopes or raised areas where water drains away quickly.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early, with fresh green succulent leaves appearing as soon as the snow melts. The plant begins spreading outward from established clumps.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is at its fullest, creating dense green mats. The spectacular orange-yellow flower display typically occurs in late summer, usually August into September.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may persist into early fall, and the succulent leaves often take on reddish or bronze tints as temperatures drop. Seeds develop in small star-shaped capsules.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, some leaves may persist, but the plant typically dies back to ground level, surviving as underground stems and roots ready to resprout in spring.

funFact: Kamchatka Stonecrop can survive being completely dried out for weeks and then spring back to life with just a little water - the succulent leaves can lose up to 80% of their water content and still recover, making it practically immortal in rock gardens!
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with other escaped stonecrop species, especially Caucasian Stonecrop which has similar growth habits. The key difference is the flower color - Kamchatka Stonecrop has distinctly orange-tinted yellow flowers, while most other stonecrops have pure yellow, white, or pink blooms.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is part of a taxonomic shuffle - it used to be classified as Sedum kamtschaticum, and you'll still see it listed that way in older field guides and garden catalogs. The genus Phedimus was split off from Sedum relatively recently, so don't be confused if you see both names used for the same plant.
compareHints: Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, Kamchatka Stonecrop stands out for its distinctly orange-tinted flowers - Caucasian Stonecrop has purer yellow or pinkish blooms, while other related species tend toward bright yellow or white. The scalloped leaf edges are also more pronounced in Kamchatka Stonecrop compared to its relatives. Its late-summer blooming time also helps distinguish it from spring-blooming stonecrop relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its stonecrop relatives, Caucasian stonecrop is distinguished by its opposite leaf arrangement and two-ranked growth pattern (leaves in two rows).
Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, yellow stonecrop is distinguished by its compact, mounded growth habit and consistently bright yellow spring flowers.
Hybrid Stonecrop has noticeably larger, more paddle-shaped leaves than its relatives like Caucasian Stonecrop, which has smaller, more rounded leaves.

Aizoon Stonecrop differs from its Phedimus relatives by having the most prominently toothed leaf margins - those little saw teeth are much more pronounced than in Caucasian Stonecrop or Kamchatka Stonecrop.
